plan: I will implement a Ridge Regression model trained on historical demand means. This approach is memory-efficient and different from the previous gradient boosting attempt. I will calculate log-transformed demand averages for various groupings (Product-Client, Product-Agency, Product, Client) using weeks 3-7, then train the Ridge model on week 8 and validate on week 9 to optimize the weights of these different mean estimates.
insight: For large-scale demand forecasting with 74M rows, computing log-transformed group mean features (Product-Client, Product-Agency, Product, Cliente) on earlier weeks and using Ridge Regression to optimally blend them achieves competitive RMSLE (~0.499) while remaining memory-efficient. The hierarchical NaN-filling strategy (mpc → mp → mc → global_mean) ensures every test row gets a reasonable estimate even for unseen combinations. This approach scales well and can be improved by adding more granular groupings (e.g., Ruta_SAK-Producto) or recent-week-weighted means.

# Facebook Recruiting Iv Human Or Bot

## Competition Description
In this competition, you'll help Facebook distinguish between human users and automated bots in online bidding systems by predicting the likelihood that a bidder is a robot. You're provided with anonymized user data including bidder IDs, payment accounts, and shipping addresses from past bidding sessions, with the goal of building a model that accurately identifies suspicious behavior. This challenge offers a real-world application of machine learning in fraud detection and user authentication, where even small improvements can significantly enhance platform security.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC), which measures the model's ability to distinguish between human and bot bidders across all classification thresholds. A higher AUC score indicates better performance in ranking positive instances (bots) higher than negative ones (humans).

Data description:
Facebook Recruiting IV: Human or Robot?

Dataset Description
This competition features two datasets: a bidder dataset containing bidder information (id, payment account, and address) and a bid dataset with 7.6 million bids made via mobile devices. 2. Bidders who may have just started their business or whose stats exceed the system-wide average, lacking clear proof of being bots.

plan: Replace the aggregation statistic from median to mean in the hierarchical backoff tables. Because the metric is RMSE, the conditional mean is the point estimator that minimizes squared error (whereas the median optimizes MAE). Always match your aggregation statistic to the loss function: mean for RMSE, median for MAE.

## Competition Description
This competition challenges participants to predict key soil functional properties using infrared spectroscopy data collected from across Africa. The dataset includes spectral measurements at various wavelengths and georeferenced information, enabling modeling of soil characteristics such as pH, organic carbon, and cation exchange capacity at unsampled locations. Accurate predictions can support sustainable land management and agricultural development in data-sparse regions, making this a critical task for environmental and food security efforts.

### Metric

Challenge:
# Facial Keypoints Detection

## Competition Description
In this challenge, you will predict the locations of key facial keypoints in grayscale images, such as eye centers, eyebrow ends, nose tip, and mouth corners. The dataset includes thousands of facial images with labeled coordinates for up to 15 keypoints, providing a realistic benchmark for facial landmark detection. This task is fundamental for applications in facial animation, emotion recognition, and human-computer interaction.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the mean squared error (MSE) between the predicted and true keypoint coordinates, averaged over all keypoints and images.

Data description:
Facial Keypoints Detection

Dataset Description
Each predicted keypoint is specified by an (x,y) real-valued pair in the space of pixel indices. There are 15 keypoints, which represent the following elements of the face:

left_eye_center, right_eye_center, left_eye_inner_corner, left_eye_outer_corner, right_eye_inner_corner, right_eye_outer_corner, left_eyebrow_inner_end, left_eyebrow_outer_end, right_eyebrow_inner_end, right_eyebrow_outer_end, nose_tip, mouth_left_corner, mouth_right_corner, mouth_center_top_lip, mouth_center_bottom_lip.

Left and right refer to the point of view of the subject. In some examples, some of the target keypoint positions are missing (encoded as missing entries in the csv, i.e., with nothing between two commas). The input image is given in the last field of the data files and consists of a list of pixels (ordered by row), as integers in (0,255). The images are 96x96 pixels.

Files
- training.csv: list of training images. Each row contains the (x,y) coordinates for 15 keypoints, and image data as a row-ordered list of pixels.
- test.csv: list of test images. Each row contains ImageId and image data as a row-ordered list of pixels.
- sample_submission.csv: list of keypoints to predict. Each row contains a RowId, ImageId, FeatureName, Location. FeatureName are "left_eye_center_x," "right_eyebrow_outer_end_y," etc. Location is what you need to predict.

Challenge:
# Yelp Recsys 2013

## Competition Description
Predict personalized business ratings for Yelp users in the Phoenix, AZ area as part of the 2013 Recommender Systems Challenge at ACM RecSys 2013. The dataset includes over 10,000 businesses and a rich collection of user reviews, ratings, and metadata, enabling the development of sophisticated recommendation models. This task offers a unique opportunity to work on real-world recommender systems using authentic user-generated content.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which measures the average difference between predicted and actual star ratings. Lower RMSE values indicate better predictive accuracy.

Data description:
RecSys2013: Yelp Business Rating Prediction

Dataset Description
The dataset provides a comprehensive overview of Yelp reviews, businesses, users, and check-ins specifically for the Phoenix, AZ metropolitan area. Participants can download either yelp_training_set.zip or yelp_training_set_mac.zip, as both contain the same files for compatibility.

Files
- Training set: yelp_training_set.zip
- Testing set: yelp_test_set.zip
- Sample submission format: sample_submission.csv

  sampleSubmissionFinal.csv (910.1 KB)

  final_test_set/ (4 items)
  yelp_test_set/ (5 items)
  yelp_training_set/ (9 items)

sampleSubmission.csv columns: RecommendationId, Stars

The dataset is organized into training and test directories containing JSON files for businesses, users, reviews, and check-ins. The IdLookupTable.csv maps RecommendationId to user and business IDs, specifying the user-business pairs for which predictions are required. Participants must predict star ratings for these pairs, with sampleSubmission.csv and sampleSubmissionFinal.csv indicating preliminary and final submission formats.

The data includes user reviews, business attributes, and star ratings, with the test set containing user-business pairs for which ratings must be predicted. The sample submission file provides the required format, listing RecommendationId and predicted Stars.

**DATASET LOCATIONS (use full paths):**
/data/dspredict-mledojo/yelp-recsys-2013

**INSTRUCTIONS:**
1. Load and explore the **training** and **test** datasets using Python (use the dataset folder location provided).
2. Perform **data preprocessing** (handling missing values, encoding, scaling, feature engineering) and **exploratory analysis** to understand distributions, correlations, and relationships between variables.
3. Where simple preprocessing and baseline models are insufficient, attempt more advanced approaches such as:
   * Model selection (e.g., tree-based models, linear models, neural networks)
   * Cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning
   * Dimensionality reduction, feature selection, or ensembling
   * Robustness checks or combining datasets if useful
4. Use the training data to build a model, evaluate it with proper validation, and then generate **predictions for the test data**.
5. Do one step at a time. Explore and validate thoroughly before moving on to model training and submission.
6. When doing exploration and data analysis, print the results in a clear and concise way.

plan: I will improve the LightGBM model by adding a "business popularity" feature: the average number of stars given to a business in the training set, weighted by the number of reviews. This differs from the `b_avg_stars` metadata as it specifically reflects the rating distribution within the training data. I will also include the "user's rating variance" to capture how much a user's ratings typically deviate from their average, which can help the model understand user-specific rating behaviors.
insight: Adding **user rating variance** (computed from training reviews as the per-user variance of star ratings) as a feature improved RMSE from 0.9653 to 0.9551. This feature captures how consistently or erratically each user rates businesses, giving the model insight into user-specific rating behavior beyond just their average stars. Compute it with `train_reviews.groupby('user_id')['stars'].var()` and fill missing values with 0 for new users.

**CHALLENGE NAME: kaggle-llm-science-exam**

Challenge:
# Kaggle Llm Science Exam

## Competition Description
In this competition, participants are challenged to predict the correct answers to complex science questions generated by a Large Language Model (LLM), inspired by the OpenBookQA dataset. The dataset contains multiple-choice questions across diverse scientific domains, and competitors must develop models to select the most accurate answer from five options (A-E). This task explores the boundaries of machine understanding in scientific reasoning and assesses whether models can outperform or align with the LLM's own answer generation, offering insights into LLM self-consistency and knowledge representation.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using Mean Average Precision at 3 (MAP@3), which measures the average precision of the model's top three predicted answers, weighted by their position and relevance. This metric emphasizes accurate ranking of correct answers within the top predictions, with higher scores given to correct answers ranked earlier.

Data description:
Kaggle - LLM Science Exam

Dataset Description
In this competition, participants will answer multiple-choice questions generated by an LLM. While the exact process for generating these questions is not disclosed, 200 sample questions with answers are provided to illustrate the format and types of questions included. However, participants should be aware of a potential distributional shift between the sample and actual test set, making broad generalization essential for success. Each question features a prompt, five options (A, B, C, D, E), and a designated correct answer. The competition employs a hidden test, where the actual test data will be revealed upon scoring submissions, consisting of approximately 4,000 unique questions.

Files
- train.csv - a set of 200 questions with the answer column
- test.csv - the test set; your task it to predict the top three most probable answers given the prompt. NOTE: the test data you see here just a copy of the training data without the answers. The unseen re-run test set is comprised of ~4,000 different prompts.
- sample_submission.csv - a sample submission file in the correct format

Available files:
  sample_submission.csv (2.1 KB)
  test.csv (180.8 KB)
  train.csv (181.3 KB)

train.csv: ~200 rows, 8 columns
Columns: id, prompt, A, B, C, D, E, answer

test.csv: ~200 rows, 7 columns

sample_submission.csv columns: id, prediction
Sample:
id,prediction
0,A B C
1,A B C

The dataset consists of a small training set (train.csv) with approximately 200 rows, each containing a question prompt, five answer choices (A-E), and the correct answer label. The test set contains additional unseen prompts, and submissions require predicting the top three most likely answers for each question.

**DATASET LOCATIONS (use full paths):**
/data/dspredict-mledojo/kaggle-llm-science-exam

**INSTRUCTIONS:**
1. Load and explore the **training** and **test** datasets using Python (use the dataset folder location provided).
2. Perform **data preprocessing** (handling missing values, encoding, scaling, feature engineering) and **exploratory analysis** to understand distributions, correlations, and relationships between variables.

   * Model selection (e.g., tree-based models, linear models, neural networks)

7. Do not use plotting libraries (assume you cannot view plots). Use text-based summaries and statistics instead.
8. When workflow tags or competition-specific guidelines are provided, you should follow them closely.
9. Only produce the **final submission and answer** when you have enough evidence and validation to support your approach.

When you finished training the best model, you should generate the final submission:

1. Use the best model to generate predictions for the test data located at the path shown above.
2. Save predictions in the required **`submission.csv` format** for the competition at /submission/submission.csv.
3. Provide a concise summary of your approach in the format: <answer>your final summary</answer>
plan: Use a non-LLM, “semantic-ish” similarity baseline by embedding texts with Latent Semantic Analysis (TruncatedSVD over TF‑IDF). We’ll compute dense vectors for the prompt and each option, then score each option by cosine similarity plus a small learned calibration using logistic regression on engineered similarity features (prompt-option sim, option length, and prompt-option TF‑IDF dot). This keeps the approach simple while capturing latent synonymy beyond raw TF‑IDF. We’ll validate with MAP@3 on a hold-out split and then train on all data to write submission.csv.
insight: Replacing raw TF-IDF text concatenation with LSA (TruncatedSVD with 200 components over TF-IDF) to compute prompt-option cosine similarity as an explicit feature improved MAP@3 from 0.458 to 0.571. Instead of feeding the full sparse TF-IDF representation directly to logistic regression, the model uses dense semantic similarity scores (LSA cosine sim, TF-IDF dot product, length features) as compact engineered features, capturing latent synonymy that raw token overlap misses.

plan: Add one targeted feature to the current LSA+calibration approach: lexical “keyword overlap” between the prompt and each option. Specifically, we’ll compute a Jaccard similarity over simple alphanumeric tokens (after lowercasing) and append it to the existing engineered feature set. This single feature often helps multiple-choice QA because correct options tend to reuse key terms from the question. We’ll keep everything else identical and re-evaluate MAP@3 on the same hold-out split before writing submission.csv.
insight: Adding a Jaccard similarity feature computed over simple alphanumeric tokens (lowercased) between the prompt and each answer option improved MAP@3 from 0.571 to 0.604. This single feature captures lexical keyword overlap that LSA cosine similarity misses, since correct answers in science MCQs frequently reuse exact terminology from the question. The fix was minimal: extract token sets for prompt and option, compute `|intersection|/|union|`, and append as a 6th feature alongside the existing LSA/TF-IDF features.

Get ready for a fun and festive competition this Thanksgiving! # Loan Default Prediction

## Competition Description
This competition challenges participants to predict the expected loss from loan defaults by estimating both the probability of default and the severity of potential losses. You are provided with historical loan data including borrower characteristics and loan performance, and your task is to predict the continuous loss value for each loan. This approach moves beyond simple binary classification, offering a more realistic and financially meaningful assessment of credit risk.

## Evaluation
### Metric

This dataset contains financial transaction records for individuals, featuring over 200,000 observations and nearly 800 features. Each observation is independent, indicating whether a default occurred and measuring the loss, which ranges from 0 to 100. The loss is normalized based on a notional value of 100, meaning a loss of 60 indicates a reimbursement of 40. If there was no default, the loss is 0. Missing feature values are retained to allow teams to utilize the full dataset and implement their own strategies for handling gaps. Some variables may be categorical (e.g., f776 and f777). The data has been standardized, de-trended, and anonymized, with the competition sponsor ensuring the removal of time-dimensionality, although training set observations are ordered chronologically while the test set is randomized.

# Grupo Bimbo Inventory Demand

## Competition Description
In this competition, you're challenged to predict the demand for over 1 million products sold by Grupo Bimbo across thousands of stores in Mexico. The dataset includes historical sales, product, client, and route information, with the goal of accurately forecasting daily demand to optimize inventory and reduce waste. This real-world problem highlights the importance of supply chain efficiency in the fast-moving consumer goods industry.

## Evaluation
### Metric
The evaluation metric is Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE), which measures the ratio between predicted and actual demand on a logarithmic scale, penalizing under- and over-predictions equally while being robust to differences in scale.

Data description:
Grupo Bimbo Inventory Demand

Dataset Description
In this competition, you will forecast the demand for a product at a specific store for a given week. The dataset includes 9 weeks of sales transactions in Mexico, with each transaction representing sales and returns. Demand for a product in a week is calculated as the sales for that week minus the returns for the following week.

The train and test datasets are time-split, along with public and private leaderboard datasets.

Key points to note:

- Some products in the test set may not appear in the train set, reflecting the dynamic nature of inventory data. Your model should adapt to this.
- Duplicate Cliente_IDs in cliente_tabla indicate that one Cliente_ID may correspond to multiple similar NombreCliente entries, necessitating data cleaning.
- Adjusted demand (Demanda_uni_equil) is always >= 0, as demand cannot be negative. Negative values for Venta_uni_hoy - Dev_uni_proxima may occur due to returns spanning multiple weeks.

# Home Depot Product Search Relevance

## Competition Description
Home Depot is seeking Kagglers to enhance the shopping experience by developing a model that accurately predicts the relevance of search results. Customers expect quick and precise results for their home improvement needs, from simple tasks like installing a ceiling fan to complex renovations. Your task is to predict the relevance score of search queries relative to product descriptions using provided query-product pairs. This challenge offers a real-world application in e-commerce search ranking, where accurate relevance prediction improves user satisfaction and engagement.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated on the root mean squared error (RMSE), which measures the square root of the average squared differences between predicted and actual relevance scores. Lower RMSE values indicate better model performance, with perfect predictions yielding an RMSE of 0.

Data description:
Home Depot Product Search Relevance

Dataset Description
This dataset includes various products and actual customer search terms from Home Depot's website. The goal is to predict a relevance score for the combinations of search terms and products. Ground truth labels were created by crowdsourcing the search/product pairs to multiple human raters. Relevance scores range from 1 (not relevant) to 3 (highly relevant). For instance, "AA battery" is highly relevant to AA batteries (3), mildly relevant to a cordless drill battery (2), and not relevant to a snow shovel (1). Each pair was evaluated by at least three raters, and the provided scores are the average of their ratings. Raters had access to product images but not to attributes, and specific instructions for the raters are included in relevance_instructions.docx.

File descriptions
- train.csv - the training set, contains products, searches, and relevance scores
- test.csv - the test set, contains products and searches. You must predict the relevance for these pairs.
- product_descriptions.csv - contains a text description of each product. You may join this table to the training or test set via the product_uid.
- attributes.csv - provides extended information about a subset of the products (typically representing detailed technical specifications). Not every product will have attributes.
- sample_submission.csv - a file showing the correct submission format
- relevance_instructions.docx - the instructions provided to human raters

Data fields
- id - a unique Id field which represents a (search_term, product_uid) pair
- product_uid - an id for the products
- product_title - the product title
- product_description - the text description of the product (may contain HTML content)
- search_term - the search query
- relevance - the average of the relevance ratings for a given id
- name - an attribute name

plan: Make one atomic improvement to the current best (Step 6): enforce monotonicity of the cumulative probabilities P(Response > k) at prediction time. Even with early stopping, the 7 independently-trained binary models can yield non-monotone outputs, which causes incoherent negative class probabilities when differenced. I will apply a simple row-wise cumulative minimum to ensure P(>1) ≥ … ≥ P(>7) before reconstructing class probabilities, then re-optimize rounding thresholds on validation and report QWK. Everything else (data prep, early stopping) stays identical.
insight: When using multiple independently-trained binary classifiers for ordinal regression (cumulative link approach), applying `np.minimum.accumulate(probs, axis=1)` row-wise after stacking predictions enforces the required monotone constraint P(y>1) ≥ P(y>2) ≥ … ≥ P(y>7). Without this, differencing non-monotone cumulative probabilities produces negative class probabilities that corrupt the expected-value continuous score used for threshold optimization. This zero-cost postprocessing step improved QWK from 0.6652 to 0.6660.

# Pubg Finish Placement Prediction

## Competition Description
Predict a player's final placement in a PUBG match based on their in-game statistics and actions. You'll be provided with a dataset of over 65,000 anonymized match instances, each containing detailed player-level features such as kills, damage dealt, movement, and team interactions. This challenge offers a fascinating look into player behavior and performance in one of the most popular battle royale games, testing your ability to extract meaningful patterns from complex, real-world gaming data.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between the predicted and actual winPlacePerc values, where winPlacePerc represents a player's finishing position as a normalized percentage (0 = last place, 1 = first place). Lower MAE indicates better predictive accuracy.

Data description:
PUBG Finish Placement Prediction (Kernels Only)

Dataset Description
In a PUBG match, up to 100 players compete, either solo or in teams, with their performance ranked based on survival. The dataset includes anonymized game stats, where each row represents a player's post-game performance. Matches can vary in player count and team size, and your goal is to create a model that predicts players' finishing placements on a scale from 1 (first place) to 0 (last place).

File descriptions
- train_V2.csv - the training set
- test_V2.csv - the test set
- sample_submission_V2.csv - a sample submission file in the correct format

Data fields
- DBNOs -  Number of enemy players knocked.
- assists -  Number of enemy players this player damaged that were killed by teammates.
- boosts -  Number of boost items used.
- damageDealt -  Total damage dealt. Note: Self inflicted damage is subtracted.
- headshotKills - Number of enemy players killed with headshots.
- heals - Number of healing items used.
- Id - Player’s Id
- killPlace -  Ranking in match of number of enemy players killed.
- killPoints - Kills-based external ranking of player. (Think of this as an Elo ranking where only kills matter.) If there is a value other than -1 in rankPoints, then any 0 in killPoints should be treated as a “None”.
- killStreaks - Max number of enemy players killed in a short amount of time.
- kills - Number of enemy players killed.
- longestKill - Longest distance between player and player killed at time of death. This may be misleading, as downing a player and driving away may lead to a large longestKill stat.
- matchDuration - Duration of match in seconds.
- matchId - ID to identify match. There are no matches that are in both the training and testing set.
- matchType - String identifying the game mode that the data comes from. The standard modes are “solo”, “duo”, “squad”, “solo-fpp”, “duo-fpp”, and “squad-fpp”; other modes are from events or custom matches.
- rankPoints - Elo-like ranking of player. This ranking is inconsistent and is being deprecated in the API’s next version, so use with caution. Value of -1 takes place of “None”.
- revives - Number of times this player revived teammates.
- rideDistance - Total distance traveled in vehicles measured in meters.
- roadKills - Number of kills while in a vehicle.
- swimDistance - Total distance traveled by swimming measured in meters.
- teamKills - Number of times this player killed a teammate.
- vehicleDestroys - Number of vehicles destroyed.
- walkDistance - Total distance traveled on foot measured in meters.
- weaponsAcquired - Number of weapons picked up.
- winPoints - Win-based external ranking of player. (Think of this as an Elo ranking where only winning matters.) If there is a value other than -1 in rankPoints, then any 0 in winPoints should be treated as a “None”.
- groupId - ID to identify a group within a match. If the same group of players plays in different matches, they will have a different groupId each time.
- numGroups - Number of groups we have data for in the match.
- maxPlace - Worst placement we have data for in the match. This may not match with numGroups, as sometimes the data skips over placements.
- winPlacePerc - The target of prediction. This is a percentile winning placement, where 1 corresponds to 1st place, and 0 corresponds to last place in the match. It is calculated off of maxPlace, not numGroups, so it is possible to have missing chunks in a match.

**CHALLENGE NAME: the-winton-stock-market-challenge**

Challenge:
# The Winton Stock Market Challenge

## Competition Description
Winton Capital invites data scientists to predict future stock returns using historical market data and anonymized features. The dataset includes thousands of rows with hundreds of features, including lagged returns and masked attributes, reflecting real-world challenges in financial forecasting. This competition offers a glimpse into the complexity of quantitative finance, where uncovering subtle, predictive signals in noisy, non-stationary data is key to success.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the Weighted Mean Absolute Error (WMAE), which measures the average absolute difference between predicted and actual returns, weighted by the importance of each sample. Lower WMAE indicates better predictive accuracy, with greater emphasis on higher-weighted predictions.

Data description:
The Winton Stock Market Challenge

Dataset Description
Updated 2015-12-21: Winton have added new data into the test set. If you downloaded the test set before 2015-12-21 please re-download the data set and submit predictions on this instead.

In this competition the challenge is to predict the return of a stock, given the history of the past few days.

We provide 5-day windows of time, days D-2, D-1, D, D+1, and D+2. You are given returns in days D-2, D-1, and part of day D, and you are asked to predict the returns in the rest of day D, and in days D+1 and D+2.

During day D, there is intraday return data, which are the returns at different points in the day. We provide 180 minutes of data, from t=1 to t=180. In the training set you are given the full 180 minutes, in the test set just the first 120 minutes are provided.

For each 5-day window, we also provide 25 features, Feature_1 to Feature_25. These may or may not be useful in your prediction.

Each row in the dataset is an arbitrary stock at an arbitrary 5 day time window.

How these returns are calculated is defined by Winton, and will not to be revealed to you in this competition. The data set is designed to be representative of real data and so should bring about a number of challenges.

File descriptions
- train.csv - the training set, including the columns of:
- test.csv - the test set, including the columns of:
- sample_submission.csv - a sample submission file in the correct format

Data fields
- Feature_1 to Feature_25: different features relevant to prediction
- Ret_MinusTwo:  this is the return from the close of trading on day D-2 to the close of trading on day D-1 (i.e. 1 day)
- Ret_MinusOne: this is the return from the close of trading on day D-1 to the point at which the intraday returns start on day D (approximately 1/2 day)
- Ret_2 to Ret_120: these are returns over approximately one minute on day D. Ret_2 is the return between t=1 and t=2.
- Ret_121 to Ret_180: intraday returns over approximately one minute on day D. These are the target variables you need to predict as {id}_{1-60}.
- Ret_PlusOne: this is the return from the time Ret_180 is measured on day D to the close of trading on day D+1. (approximately 1day). This is a target variable you need to predict as {id}_61.
- Ret_PlusTwo: this is the return from the close of trading on day D+1 to the close of trading on day D+2 (i.e. 1 day) This is a target variable you need to predict as {id}_62.
- Weight_Intraday: weight used to evaluate intraday return predictions Ret 121 to 180
- Weight_Daily: weight used to evaluate daily return predictions (Ret_PlusOne and Ret_PlusTwo).

Available files:
  sample_submission_2.csv (88.8 MB)
  test_2.csv (288.5 MB)
  train.csv (177.2 MB)
  __MACOSX/ (3 items)

train.csv: ~40,000 rows, 211 columns
Columns (first 20): Id, Feature_1, Feature_2, Feature_3, Feature_4, Feature_5, Feature_6, Feature_7, Feature_8, Feature_9, Feature_10, Feature_11, Feature_12, Feature_13, Feature_14, Feature_15, Feature_16, Feature_17, Feature_18, Feature_19, ... (191 more)

The training set contains approximately 40,000 rows and 211 columns, including anonymized features and a sequence of lagged returns ranging from Ret_MinusTwo to Ret_159, with the target likely being a forward-looking return not explicitly shown in the sample.

**DATASET LOCATIONS (use full paths):**
/data/dspredict-mledojo/the-winton-stock-market-challenge

**INSTRUCTIONS:**
1. Load and explore the **training** and **test** datasets using Python (use the dataset folder location provided).
2. Perform **data preprocessing** (handling missing values, encoding, scaling, feature engineering) and **exploratory analysis** to understand distributions, correlations, and relationships between variables.
3. Where simple preprocessing and baseline models are insufficient, attempt more advanced approaches such as:
   * Model selection (e.g., tree-based models, linear models, neural networks)
   * Cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning
   * Dimensionality reduction, feature selection, or ensembling
   * Robustness checks or combining datasets if useful
4. Use the training data to build a model, evaluate it with proper validation, and then generate **predictions for the test data**.
5. Do one step at a time. Explore and validate thoroughly before moving on to model training and submission.
6. When doing exploration and data analysis, print the results in a clear and concise way.
7. Do not use plotting libraries (assume you cannot view plots). Use text-based summaries and statistics instead.

When you finished training the best model, you should generate the final submission:

1. Use the best model to generate predictions for the test data located at the path shown above.
2. Save predictions in the required **`submission.csv` format** for the competition at /submission/submission.csv.
3. Provide a concise summary of your approach in the format: <answer>your final summary</answer>
plan: Keep the solution extremely lightweight to avoid kernel instability: use a per-target baseline that predicts each future return as the mean of the last few observed intraday returns (momentum/continuation proxy), with a fallback to zero if needed. This is “model-free”, fast, and still uses validation with the official WMAE metric. Then generate test predictions using the same rule and write submission.csv in the exact sample_submission_2.csv format. This avoids heavy training while producing a valid, competitive-enough baseline under resource constraints.
insight: For this competition, predicting intraday returns (Ret_121–180) as the mean of the last k observed intraday returns (Ret_2–120) provides a surprisingly strong baseline with WMAE ~0.00121, outperforming naive zero-prediction. The key insight is that recent intraday momentum/continuation is the dominant signal, while daily targets (Ret_PlusOne, Ret_PlusTwo) benefit from dampening (0.5× and 0× scaling respectively) since mean-reversion dominates at longer horizons.

# The Winton Stock Market Challenge

## Competition Description
Winton Capital invites data scientists to predict future stock returns using historical market data and anonymized features. The dataset includes thousands of rows with hundreds of features, including lagged returns and masked attributes, reflecting real-world challenges in financial forecasting. This competition offers a glimpse into the complexity of quantitative finance, where uncovering subtle, predictive signals in noisy, non-stationary data is key to success.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the Weighted Mean Absolute Error (WMAE), which measures the average absolute difference between predicted and actual returns, weighted by the importance of each sample. Lower WMAE indicates better predictive accuracy, with greater emphasis on higher-weighted predictions.

Data description:
The Winton Stock Market Challenge

Dataset Description
Updated 2015-12-21: Winton have added new data into the test set. If you downloaded the test set before 2015-12-21 please re-download the data set and submit predictions on this instead.

In this competition the challenge is to predict the return of a stock, given the history of the past few days.

We provide 5-day windows of time, days D-2, D-1, D, D+1, and D+2. You are given returns in days D-2, D-1, and part of day D, and you are asked to predict the returns in the rest of day D, and in days D+1 and D+2.

During day D, there is intraday return data, which are the returns at different points in the day. We provide 180 minutes of data, from t=1 to t=180. In the training set you are given the full 180 minutes, in the test set just the first 120 minutes are provided.

For each 5-day window, we also provide 25 features, Feature_1 to Feature_25. These may or may not be useful in your prediction.

Each row in the dataset is an arbitrary stock at an arbitrary 5 day time window.

How these returns are calculated is defined by Winton, and will not to be revealed to you in this competition. The data set is designed to be representative of real data and so should bring about a number of challenges.

File descriptions
- train.csv - the training set, including the columns of:
- test.csv - the test set, including the columns of:

Data fields

- Ret_MinusTwo:  this is the return from the close of trading on day D-2 to the close of trading on day D-1 (i.e. 1 day)
- Ret_MinusOne: this is the return from the close of trading on day D-1 to the point at which the intraday returns start on day D (approximately 1/2 day)
- Ret_2 to Ret_120: these are returns over approximately one minute on day D. Ret_2 is the return between t=1 and t=2.
- Ret_121 to Ret_180: intraday returns over approximately one minute on day D. These are the target variables you need to predict as {id}_{1-60}.

- Ret_PlusTwo: this is the return from the close of trading on day D+1 to the close of trading on day D+2 (i.e. 1 day) This is a target variable you need to predict as {id}_62.

## Competition Description
In this engaging recruiting competition, participants are challenged to forecast weekly sales for various departments across 45 Walmart stores using historical sales data. Accurate forecasts will help Walmart better understand and plan for demand fluctuations during critical shopping periods.

### Metric
The competition is evaluated using the weighted mean absolute error (WMAE), which assigns higher weights to holiday weeks. This emphasizes the importance of accurately predicting sales during peak shopping periods, aligning the model's performance with real-world business needs.

Challenge:
# Home Depot Product Search Relevance

## Competition Description
Home Depot is seeking Kagglers to enhance the shopping experience by developing a model that accurately predicts the relevance of search results. Customers expect quick and precise results for their home improvement needs, from simple tasks like installing a ceiling fan to complex renovations. Your task is to predict the relevance score of search queries relative to product descriptions using provided query-product pairs. This challenge offers a real-world application in e-commerce search ranking, where accurate relevance prediction improves user satisfaction and engagement.

### Metric
Submissions are evaluated on the root mean squared error (RMSE), which measures the square root of the average squared differences between predicted and actual relevance scores. Lower RMSE values indicate better model performance, with perfect predictions yielding an RMSE of 0.

Home Depot Product Search Relevance

This dataset includes various products and actual customer search terms from Home Depot's website. The goal is to predict a relevance score for the combinations of search terms and products. Ground truth labels were created by crowdsourcing the search/product pairs to multiple human raters. Relevance scores range from 1 (not relevant) to 3 (highly relevant). For instance, "AA battery" is highly relevant to AA batteries (3), mildly relevant to a cordless drill battery (2), and not relevant to a snow shovel (1). Each pair was evaluated by at least three raters, and the provided scores are the average of their ratings. Raters had access to product images but not to attributes, and specific instructions for the raters are included in relevance_instructions.docx.

- relevance_instructions.docx - the instructions provided to human raters

- id - a unique Id field which represents a (search_term, product_uid) pair
- product_uid - an id for the products
- product_title - the product title

Predict whether Kobe Bryant made or missed each shot during his NBA career based on detailed game and shot information. Submissions are evaluated using log loss, which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities. Lower log loss indicates better-calibrated probability estimates, penalizing overconfident wrong predictions more severely.

### Metric

# Battlefin S Big Data Combine Forecasting Challenge

## Competition Description
The Big Data Combine, created by BattleFin, is a predictive modeling challenge that invites data scientists to forecast percentage changes in financial outcomes using rich sentiment data. Participants will analyze large-scale datasets containing sentiment signals across multiple time points to predict future movements. This competition offers a unique opportunity to apply machine learning expertise to real-world financial forecasting, where accuracy can translate into tangible trading advantages.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), which measures the average absolute difference between predicted and actual percentage changes. Lower MAE values indicate better predictive performance.

Data description:
The Big Data Combine Engineered by BattleFin

Dataset Description
For this competition, you are asked to predict the percentage change in a financial instrument at a time 2 hours in the future. The data represents features of various financial securities (198 in total) recorded at 5-minute intervals throughout a trading day. To discourage cheating, you are not provided with the features' names or the specific dates.

data.zip - contains features for 510 days worth of trading, including 200 training days and 310 testing days  
trainLabels.csv - contains the targets for the 200 training days  
sampleSubmission.csv - shows the submission format  

Each variable named O1, O2, O3, etc. (the outputs) represents a percent change in the value of a security. Each variable named I1, I2, I3, etc. (the inputs) represents a feature. The underlying securities and features represented by these anonymized names are the same across all files (e.g. O1 will always be the same stock).

Within each trading day, you are provided the outputs as a relative percentage compared to the previous day's closing price. The first line of each data file represents the previous close. For example, if a security closed at $1 the previous day and opened at $2 the next day, the first output would be 0, then 100. All output values are computed relative to the previous day's close. The timestamps within each file are as follows (ignoring the header row):

Line 1 = Outputs and inputs at previous day's close (4PM ET)  
Line 2 = Outputs and inputs at current day's open (9:30AM ET)  
Line 3 = Outputs and inputs at 9:35AM ET...  
Line 55 = Outputs and inputs at 1:55PM ET  

You are asked to predict the outputs 2 hours later, at 4PM ET.

Challenge:
# Amazon Employee Access Challenge

## Competition Description
In this competition, participants are challenged to predict whether an employee should be granted access to a particular resource based on their role and organizational attributes. The dataset includes anonymized features representing employee roles, departments, management chains, and resource identifiers, with the target variable indicating approved access. This task reflects real-world IT access management challenges and offers insight into automating secure and efficient access control decisions.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), which measures the model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes. A higher AUC indicates better performance in ranking predictions by confidence.

Data description:
Amazon.com - Employee Access Challenge

Dataset Description
The dataset comprises real historical data from 2010 and 2011, detailing how employees were manually granted or denied access to resources over time. Participants must develop an algorithm that learns from this data to predict access approvals or denials for a new set of employees.

File Descriptions
train.csv - The training set. Each row has the ACTION (ground truth), RESOURCE, and information about the employee's role at the time of approval.

test.csv - The test set for which predictions should be made. Each row asks whether an employee having the listed characteristics should have access to the listed resource.

Column Descriptions
| Column Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ACTION | ACTION is 1 if the resource was approved, 0 if the resource was not |
| RESOURCE | An ID for each resource |
| MGR_ID | The EMPLOYEE ID of the manager of the current EMPLOYEE ID record; an employee may have only one manager at a time |
| ROLE_ROLLUP_1 | Company role grouping category id 1 (e.g. US Engineering) |
| ROLE_ROLLUP_2 | Company role grouping category id 2 (e.g. US Retail) |
| ROLE_DEPTNAME | Company role department description (e.g. Retail) |
| ROLE_TITLE | Company role business title description (e.g. Senior Engineering Retail Manager) |
| ROLE_FAMILY_DESC | Company role family extended description (e.g. Retail Manager, Software Engineering) |
| ROLE_FAMILY | Company role family description (e.g. Retail Manager) |

Challenge:
# Poker Rule Induction

## Competition Description
In this competition, you'll predict the best possible poker hand from a set of five playing cards, where each row represents a unique hand. The dataset includes card suits and values in order, and your task is to classify each hand into the correct poker category such as straight flush, four of a kind, or pair. This challenge blends rule-based reasoning with machine learning, offering a fun and educational benchmark for pattern recognition and combinatorial logic.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using classification accuracy, which measures the percentage of poker hands correctly predicted in the test set.

Data description:
Poker Rule Induction

Dataset Description
You are provided with 25,010 poker hands in train.csv and 1,000,000 in test.csv. Each hand consists of five cards with a given suit and rank, drawn from a standard deck of 52. Suits and ranks are represented as ordinal categories:

```
S1 “Suit of card #1”
Ordinal (1-4) representing {Hearts, Spades, Diamonds, Clubs}
C1 “Rank of card #1”
Numerical (1-13) representing (Ace, 2, 3, ... , Queen, King)
...

S5 “Suit of card #5”
C5 “Rank of card #5”
```

Each row in the training set has the accompanying class label for the poker hand it comprises. The hands are omitted from the test set and must be predicted by participants. Hands are classified into the following ordinal categories:

```
0: Nothing in hand; not a recognized poker hand 
1: One pair; one pair of equal ranks within five cards
2: Two pairs; two pairs of equal ranks within five cards
3: Three of a kind; three equal ranks within five cards
4: Straight; five cards, sequentially ranked with no gaps
5: Flush; five cards with the same suit
6: Full house; pair + different rank three of a kind
7: Four of a kind; four equal ranks within five cards
8: Straight flush; straight + flush
9: Royal flush; {Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Ten} + flush
```

Note that the Straight flush and Royal flush hands are not representative of the true domain because they have been over-sampled. The straight flush is 14.43 times more likely to occur in the training set, while the royal flush is 129.82 times more likely.

plan:
I'll create a solution that takes a more rule-based approach combined with machine learning. Instead of just counting ranks and suits, I'll implement explicit poker hand detection logic that directly identifies hand types based on poker rules. This approach will:
1. Load and preprocess the data
2. Create features using explicit poker hand detection algorithms
3. Use a Gradient Boosting classifier to learn from these rule-based features
4. Evaluate using cross-validation

insight: Implementing a deterministic rule-based poker hand classifier as a feature (`detected_hand`) — rather than relying on the ML model to infer hand types from rank/suit counts — was the key improvement. This single feature directly encodes the correct answer for most hands, reducing the model's job to correcting edge cases. The GradientBoosting model then only needs to handle rare ambiguities, explaining the jump from 0.9996 to 0.99996.

## Competition Description
Predict the level of risk associated with home insurance policies based on property features and historical data. Liberty Mutual Insurance provides a dataset of over 50,000 properties with anonymized categorical and numerical variables, where the goal is to predict a transformed count of hazards or pre-existing damages. The goal of the competition is to forecast the hazard score based on anonymized variables available prior to ordering an inspection.

Challenge:
# The Winton Stock Market Challenge

## Competition Description
Winton Capital invites data scientists to predict future stock returns using historical market data and anonymized features. The dataset includes thousands of rows with hundreds of features, including lagged returns and masked attributes, reflecting real-world challenges in financial forecasting. This competition offers a glimpse into the complexity of quantitative finance, where uncovering subtle, predictive signals in noisy, non-stationary data is key to success.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using the Weighted Mean Absolute Error (WMAE), which measures the average absolute difference between predicted and actual returns, weighted by the importance of each sample. Lower WMAE indicates better predictive accuracy, with greater emphasis on higher-weighted predictions.

Data description:
The Winton Stock Market Challenge

Dataset Description
Updated 2015-12-21: Winton have added new data into the test set. If you downloaded the test set before 2015-12-21 please re-download the data set and submit predictions on this instead.

In this competition the challenge is to predict the return of a stock, given the history of the past few days.

We provide 5-day windows of time, days D-2, D-1, D, D+1, and D+2. You are given returns in days D-2, D-1, and part of day D, and you are asked to predict the returns in the rest of day D, and in days D+1 and D+2.

During day D, there is intraday return data, which are the returns at different points in the day. We provide 180 minutes of data, from t=1 to t=180. In the training set you are given the full 180 minutes, in the test set just the first 120 minutes are provided.

For each 5-day window, we also provide 25 features, Feature_1 to Feature_25. These may or may not be useful in your prediction.

Each row in the dataset is an arbitrary stock at an arbitrary 5 day time window.

How these returns are calculated is defined by Winton, and will not to be revealed to you in this competition. The data set is designed to be representative of real data and so should bring about a number of challenges.

- train.csv - the training set, including the columns of:
- test.csv - the test set, including the columns of:

Data fields
- Feature_1 to Feature_25: different features relevant to prediction
- Ret_MinusTwo:  this is the return from the close of trading on day D-2 to the close of trading on day D-1 (i.e. 1 day)
- Ret_MinusOne: this is the return from the close of trading on day D-1 to the point at which the intraday returns start on day D (approximately 1/2 day)
- Ret_2 to Ret_120: these are returns over approximately one minute on day D. Ret_2 is the return between t=1 and t=2.
- Ret_121 to Ret_180: intraday returns over approximately one minute on day D. These are the target variables you need to predict as {id}_{1-60}.
- Ret_PlusOne: this is the return from the time Ret_180 is measured on day D to the close of trading on day D+1. (approximately 1day). This is a target variable you need to predict as {id}_61.
- Ret_PlusTwo: this is the return from the close of trading on day D+1 to the close of trading on day D+2 (i.e. 1 day) This is a target variable you need to predict as {id}_62.
- Weight_Intraday: weight used to evaluate intraday return predictions Ret 121 to 180
- Weight_Daily: weight used to evaluate daily return predictions (Ret_PlusOne and Ret_PlusTwo).

Challenge:
# Rossmann Store Sales

## Competition Description
Rossmann, a leading drug store chain with over 3,000 locations across 7 European countries, is inviting participants to predict daily sales for 1,115 stores in Germany over a six-week period. Store managers currently face challenges in forecasting sales due to various influencing factors such as promotions, holidays, and day of the week. Accurate sales predictions can help optimize staffing, inventory, and improve overall operational efficiency.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated on the Root Mean Square Percentage Error (RMSPE), which measures the root mean square of the percentage differences between predicted and actual sales. Lower RMSPE values indicate better predictive accuracy relative to the true sales values.

Data description:
Rossmann Store Sales

Dataset Description
You are provided with historical sales data for 1,115 Rossmann stores. The task is to forecast the "Sales" column for the test set. Note that some stores in the dataset were temporarily closed for refurbishment.

Files
- train.csv - historical data including Sales
- test.csv - historical data excluding Sales
- sample_submission.csv - a sample submission file in the correct format
- store.csv - supplemental information about the stores

Data fields
Most of the fields are self-explanatory. The following are descriptions for those that aren't.

- Id - an Id that represents a (Store, Date) duple within the test set
- Store - a unique Id for each store
- Sales - the turnover for any given day (this is what you are predicting)
- Customers - the number of customers on a given day
- Open - an indicator for whether the store was open: 0 = closed, 1 = open
- StateHoliday - indicates a state holiday. Normally all stores, with few exceptions, are closed on state holidays. Note that all schools are closed on public holidays and weekends. a = public holiday, b = Easter holiday, c = Christmas, 0 = None
- SchoolHoliday - indicates if the (Store, Date) was affected by the closure of public schools
- StoreType - differentiates between 4 different store models: a, b, c, d
- Assortment - describes an assortment level: a = basic, b = extra, c = extended
- CompetitionDistance - distance in meters to the nearest competitor store
- CompetitionOpenSince[Month/Year] - gives the approximate year and month of the time the nearest competitor was opened
- Promo - indicates whether a store is running a promo on that day
- Promo2 - Promo2 is a continuing and consecutive promotion for some stores: 0 = store is not participating, 1 = store is participating
- Promo2Since[Year/Week] - describes the year and calendar week when the store started participating in Promo2
- PromoInterval - describes the consecutive intervals Promo2 is started, naming the months the promotion is started anew. E.g. "Feb,May,Aug,Nov" means each round starts in February, May, August, November of any given year for that store

## Competition Description
In this engaging recruiting competition, participants are challenged to forecast weekly sales for various departments across 45 Walmart stores using historical sales data. Accurate forecasts will help Walmart better understand and plan for demand fluctuations during critical shopping periods.

## Evaluation
### Metric
The competition is evaluated using the weighted mean absolute error (WMAE), which assigns higher weights to holiday weeks. This emphasizes the importance of accurately predicting sales during peak shopping periods, aligning the model's performance with real-world business needs.

Data description:

Dataset Description
You are provided with historical sales data for 45 Walmart stores located in different regions. Each store contains a number of departments, and you are tasked with predicting the department-wide sales for each store. Additionally, Walmart runs several promotional markdown events throughout the year, particularly around major holidays such as the Super Bowl, Labor Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas. Challenge:
# Unimelb

## Competition Description
The University of Melbourne is hosting a competition to predict the success of research grant applications, a critical challenge given the declining funding success rates of around 20-25%. Participants will use historical application data including researcher profiles, project details, and funding outcomes to build predictive models. This task offers a unique opportunity to contribute to improving research funding efficiency and fairness using real-world academic data.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions will be evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which measures the model's ability to distinguish between successful and unsuccessful grant applications. A higher AUC indicates better performance in ranking positive instances higher than negative ones.

Data description:
Predict Grant Applications

Dataset Description
This dataset includes 249 features (or predictors). Participants should use these variables to predict the target variable (or outcome), "Grant Status". A grant status of 1 represents a successful grant application, while a grant status of 0 represents an unsuccessful application. The training dataset, which participants use to build their models, is unimelb_training.csv. It contains 8,707 grant applications from late 2005 to 2008. Challenge:
# Sf Crime

## Competition Description
In this challenge, you are tasked with predicting the category of crime incidents in San Francisco based on historical data. The dataset includes features such as the time, location, and police district of each incident, and your goal is to classify each into one of several crime categories. This problem highlights the intersection of urban dynamics and machine learning, offering insights into public safety and socio-economic trends in a major U.S. city.

## Evaluation
### Metric
Submissions are evaluated using multi-class logarithmic loss, which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities for each crime category. Lower log loss indicates better-calibrated probability estimates, with emphasis on confident and correct predictions.

Data description:
San Francisco Crime Classification

Dataset Description
This dataset contains incidents derived from the SFPD Crime Incident Reporting system, covering the period from 1/1/2003 to 5/13/2015. The training and test sets rotate weekly, with odd weeks designated for testing and even weeks for training.

# Digit Recognizer

## Competition Description

Start here if...  
You have some experience with R or Python and machine learning basics, but you're new to computer vision. This competition is the perfect introduction to techniques like neural networks using a classic dataset including pre-extracted features.

MNIST ("Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology") is the de facto "hello world" dataset of computer vision. Since its release in 1999, this classic dataset of handwritten images has served as the basis for benchmarking classification algorithms. As new machine learning techniques emerge, MNIST remains a reliable resource for researchers and learners alike.

In this competition, your goal is to correctly identify digits from a dataset of tens of thousands of handwritten images. We've curated a set of tutorial-style kernels which cover everything from regression to neural networks. We encourage you to experiment with different algorithms to learn first-hand what works well and how techniques compare.

### Practice Skills
- Computer vision fundamentals including simple neural networks
- Classification methods such as SVM and K-nearest neighbors

### Acknowledgements
More details about the dataset, including algorithms that have been tried on it and their levels of success, can be found at http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/index.html. The dataset is made available under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 license.

## Tutorial

### Kaggle Learn
Kaggle Learn offers hands-on courses for most data science topics. These short courses prepare you with everything you need to start your own projects, including deep learning and computer vision projects.

The Deep Learning Course will give you everything you need to succeed in this competition and others like it.

### Other Python Tutorials
- Deep neural network the Keras way
  - Covers pre-processing including feature standardization and one-hot encoding
  - Implements an artificial neural network approach using Keras
- Simple deep MLP with Keras
  - A straightforward implementation of MLP (multi-layer perceptron) in Keras
  - Learn Keras from the author himself, Francois Chollet!
- An introduction to dimensionality reduction
  - Introduces and compares PCA, LDA, and t-SNE dimensionality reduction techniques
  - Uses the Plotly library for intuitive, interactive visualizations

### Other R Tutorials
- Random forest benchmark
  - A minimal example implementing the random forest algorithm
- Build your own neural network in R
  - Implements a simple 2-layer neural network from scratch
  - Based on the CS231n course offered by Stanford
- Minimum distance classifier
  - Uses minimum distance as a simple approach to classification

## Evaluation

### Goal
The goal in this competition is to take an image of a handwritten single digit, and determine what that digit is. For every image in the test set, you should predict the correct label.

### Metric
This competition is evaluated on the categorization accuracy of your predictions (the percentage of images you get correct).

### Submission File Format
The file should contain a header and have the following format:
```
ImageId,Label
1,0
2,0
3,0
etc.
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a Getting Started competition?
Getting Started competitions were created by Kaggle data scientists for people who have little to no machine learning background. They are a great place to begin if you are new to data science or just finished a MOOC and want to get involved in Kaggle.

Getting Started competitions are a non-competitive way to get familiar with Kaggle's platform, learn basic machine learning concepts, and start meeting people in the community. They have no cash prize and are on a rolling timeline.

### How do I create and manage a team?
When you accept the competition rules, a team will be created for you. You can invite others to your team, accept a merger with another team, and update basic information like team name by going to the Team page.

We've heard from many Kagglers that teaming up is the best way to learn new skills AND have fun. If you don't have a teammate already, consider asking if anyone wants to team up in the discussion forum.

### What are Notebooks?
Kaggle Notebooks is a cloud computational environment that enables reproducible and collaborative analysis. Kernels supports scripts in R and Python, Jupyter Notebooks, and RMarkdown reports. Go to the Notebooks tab to view all of the publicly shared code on this competition. For more on how to use Notebooks to learn data science, visit Kaggle's Learn Courses.

### What's the difference between a private and public leaderboard?
In this competition, because it is a Getting Started competition, there is no difference. We're scoring the entire test set on the Public Leaderboard. And we will refresh the competition every three months, so the Private Leaderboard is irrelevant.

For non-Getting Started Kaggle competitions, there is the concept of a public and private leaderboard to prevent participants from "overfitting" to the leaderboard. If your model is "overfit" to a dataset then it is not generalizable outside of the dataset you trained it on. This means that your model would have low accuracy on another sample of data taken from a similar dataset.

### Why are there perfect scores on the leaderboard?
This competition's test set labels are completely public. So it's likely that some participants will submit perfect submissions. Since there are no prizes, medals, or points associated with your leaderboard ranking in this competition, these scores have little consequence. The rankings are purely for the benefit of users to learn and see how their approach is improving.

"It's a heavily time-intensive process to manage removals from a continuously live leaderboard. The threshold for what should be removed also becomes arbitrary -- if you remove 1.00 scores, then .99 scores will quickly appear. Since there is no prize consequence, we have chosen to leave the scores as an open sandbox."

### Why did my team disappear from the leaderboard?
To keep with the spirit of getting-started competitions, we have implemented a two month rolling window on submissions. Once a submission is more than two months old, it will be invalidated and no longer count towards the leaderboard.

If your team has no submissions in the previous two months, the team will also drop from the leaderboard. This will keep the leaderboard at a manageable size, freshen it up, and prevent newcomers from getting lost in a sea of abandoned scores.

### How do I contact Support?
Kaggle does not have a dedicated support team so you'll typically find that you receive a response more quickly by asking your question in the appropriate forum. (For this competition, you'll want to use this competition's discussion forum.)

Support is only able to help with issues that are being experienced by all participants. Before contacting support, please check the discussion forum for information on your problem. The forums are full of useful information on the data, metric, and different approaches. We encourage you to use the forums often. If you share your knowledge, you'll find that others will share a lot in turn!

If your problem persists or it seems to be affecting all participants then please contact us.

Dataset Description
The data files train.csv and test.csv contain gray-scale images of hand-drawn digits, from zero through nine.
Each image is 28 pixels in height and 28 pixels in width, for a total of 784 pixels in total. Each pixel has a single pixel-value associated with it, indicating the lightness or darkness of that pixel, with higher numbers meaning darker. This pixel-value is an integer between 0 and 255, inclusive.
The training data set, (train.csv), has 785 columns. The first column, called "label", is the digit that was drawn by the user. The rest of the columns contain the pixel-values of the associated image.
Each pixel column in the training set has a name like pixelx, where x is an integer between 0 and 783, inclusive. To locate this pixel on the image, suppose that we have decomposed x as x = i * 28 + j, where i and j are integers between 0 and 27, inclusive. Then pixelx is located on row i and column j of a 28 x 28 matrix, (indexing by zero).
For example, pixel31 indicates the pixel that is in the fourth column from the left, and the second row from the top, as in the ascii-diagram below.
Visually, if we omit the "pixel" prefix, the pixels make up the image like this:
000 001 002 003 ... 026 027
028 029 030 031 ... 054 055
056 057 058 059 ... 082 083

728 729 730 731 ... 754 755
756 757 758 759 ... 782 783

The test data set, (test.csv), is the same as the training set, except that it does not contain the "label" column.

3,8

### What is a Getting Started competition?
Getting Started competitions were created by Kaggle data scientists for people who have little to no machine learning background. They are a great place to begin if you are new to data science or just finished a MOOC and want to get involved in Kaggle.

Getting Started competitions are a non-competitive way to get familiar with Kaggle's platform, learn basic machine learning concepts, and start meeting people in the community. They have no cash prize and are on a rolling timeline.

### What are Notebooks?
Kaggle Notebooks is a cloud computational environment that enables reproducible and collaborative analysis. Kernels supports scripts in R and Python, Jupyter Notebooks, and RMarkdown reports. Go to the Notebooks tab to view all of the publicly shared code on this competition. For more on how to use Notebooks to learn data science, visit Kaggle's Learn Courses.

### What's the difference between a private and public leaderboard?
In this competition, because it is a Getting Started competition, there is no difference. We're scoring the entire test set on the Public Leaderboard. And we will refresh the competition every three months, so the Private Leaderboard is irrelevant.

For non-Getting Started Kaggle competitions, there is the concept of a public and private leaderboard to prevent participants from "overfitting" to the leaderboard. If your model is "overfit" to a dataset then it is not generalizable outside of the dataset you trained it on. This means that your model would have low accuracy on another sample of data taken from a similar dataset.

### Why are there perfect scores on the leaderboard?
This competition's test set labels are completely public. So it's likely that some participants will submit perfect submissions. Since there are no prizes, medals, or points associated with your leaderboard ranking in this competition, these scores have little consequence. ### Why did my team disappear from the leaderboard?
To keep with the spirit of getting-started competitions, we have implemented a two month rolling window on submissions. Once a submission is more than two months old, it will be invalidated and no longer count towards the leaderboard.

If your team has no submissions in the previous two months, the team will also drop from the leaderboard. This will keep the leaderboard at a manageable size, freshen it up, and prevent newcomers from getting lost in a sea of abandoned scores.

Kaggle does not have a dedicated support team so you'll typically find that you receive a response more quickly by asking your question in the appropriate forum. (For this competition, you'll want to use this competition's discussion forum.)

Dataset Description
The data files train.csv and test.csv contain gray-scale images of hand-drawn digits, from zero through nine.
Each image is 28 pixels in height and 28 pixels in width, for a total of 784 pixels in total. Each pixel has a single pixel-value associated with it, indicating the lightness or darkness of that pixel, with higher numbers meaning darker. This pixel-value is an integer between 0 and 255, inclusive.
The training data set, (train.csv), has 785 columns. The first column, called "label", is the digit that was drawn by the user. The rest of the columns contain the pixel-values of the associated image.
Each pixel column in the training set has a name like pixelx, where x is an integer between 0 and 783, inclusive. To locate this pixel on the image, suppose that we have decomposed x as x = i * 28 + j, where i and j are integers between 0 and 27, inclusive. Then pixelx is located on row i and column j of a 28 x 28 matrix, (indexing by zero).
For example, pixel31 indicates the pixel that is in the fourth column from the left, and the second row from the top, as in the ascii-diagram below.
Visually, if we omit the "pixel" prefix, the pixels make up the image like this:
000 001 002 003 ... 026 027
028 029 030 031 ... 054 055
056 057 058 059 ... 082 083
 |   |   |   |  ...  |   |
728 729 730 731 ... 754 755
756 757 758 759 ... 782 783

The test data set, (test.csv), is the same as the training set, except that it does not contain the "label" column.

Your submission file should be in the following format: For each of the 28000 images in the test set, output a single line containing the ImageId and the digit you predict. For example, if you predict that the first image is of a 3, the second image is of a 7, and the third image is of a 8, then your submission file would look like:
ImageId,Label
1,3
2,7
3,8 
(27997 more lines)

The evaluation metric for this contest is the categorization accuracy, or the proportion of test images that are correctly classified. For example, a categorization accuracy of 0.97 indicates that you have correctly classified all but 3% of the images.

plan: Make one atomic improvement focused on feature robustness: apply a light Gaussian smoothing to the 28×28 images before computing gradients. This reduces pixel-level noise and makes gradient orientations more stable, which can help linear classifiers on HOG-like features. We’ll keep the same cell_size=4, nbins=8 extractor and LinearSVC settings as the best approach, only adding a fixed 3×3 Gaussian blur preprocessing step. insight: Adding a light fixed 3×3 Gaussian blur (kernel [[1,2,1],[2,4,2],[1,2,1]]/16 with reflect padding) to each 28×28 image before computing HOG-like gradients improved accuracy. plan: The timeout came from the PolynomialFeatures expansion creating a very large design matrix and making ElasticNet fitting slow. Keep the same overall linear+polynomial idea, but constrain feature growth by (1) using degree=2 with interaction_only=True, (2) limiting polynomial expansion to a subset of numeric columns (excluding id and restricting to at most 20 columns), and (3) switching to SGDRegressor with elastic-net penalty, which scales much better to large sparse matrices. plan: Make one atomic improvement by increasing the tree expressiveness of HistGradientBoostingRegressor via `max_leaf_nodes`. **CHALLENGE NAME: house-prices-advanced-regression-techniques**

Challenge:
# House Prices - Advanced Regression Techniques

Predict sales prices and practice feature engineering, RFs, and gradient boosting

## Competition Description
Ask a home buyer to describe their dream house, and they probably won't begin with the height of the basement ceiling or the proximity to an east-west railroad. But this playground competition's dataset proves that much more influences price negotiations than the number of bedrooms or a white-picket fence.

With 79 explanatory variables describing (almost) every aspect of residential homes in Ames, Iowa, this competition challenges you to predict the final price of each home.

### Practice Skills
- Creative feature engineering
- Advanced regression techniques like random forest and gradient boosting

## Evaluation
### Goal
It is your job to predict the sales price for each house. For each Id in the test set, you must predict the value of the SalePrice variable.

### Metric
Submissions are evaluated on Root-Mean-Squared-Error (RMSE) between the logarithm of the predicted value and the logarithm of the observed sales price. (Taking logs means that errors in predicting expensive houses and cheap houses will affect the result equally.)

### Submission File Format
The file should contain a header and have the following format:
Id,SalePrice
1461,169000.1
1462,187724.1233
1463,175221
etc.

You can download an example submission file (sample_submission.csv) on the Data page.

## Competition Details
- **Competition Host**: Kaggle
- **Prizes & Awards**: Does not award Points or Medals
- **Participation**: 901,161 Entrants, 4,175 Participants, 4,079 Teams, 18,059 Submissions
- **Tags**: Regression, Tabular, Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error
- **Timeline**: This competition runs indefinitely with a rolling leaderboard

House Prices - Advanced Regression Techniques
Predict sales prices and practice feature engineering, RFs, and gradient boosting

Dataset Description
File descriptions

Data fields
Here's a brief version of what you'll find in the data description file.
SalePrice - the property's sale price in dollars. This is the target variable that you're trying to predict.
MSSubClass: The building class
MSZoning: The general zoning classification
LotFrontage: Linear feet of street connected to property
LotArea: Lot size in square feet
Street: Type of road access
Alley: Type of alley access
LotShape: General shape of property

Condition1: Proximity to main road or railroad

OverallQual: Overall material and finish quality

Exterior2nd: Exterior covering on house (if more than one material)

Foundation: Type of foundation

Challenge description:
Playground Series - Season 5, Episode 3

Welcome to the 2025 Kaggle Playground Series! We plan to continue in the spirit of previous playgrounds, providing interesting and approachable datasets for our community to practice their machine learning skills, and anticipate a competition each month.

Your Goal: Your goal is to predict rainfall for each day of the year.

Submissions are evaluated on area under the ROC curve between the predicted probability and the observed target.

For each id in the test set, you must predict a probability for the target rainfall. The file should contain a header and have the following format: id,rainfall2190,0.52191,0.12192,0.9etc.

Start Date- March 1, 2025
Entry Deadline- Same as the Final Submission Deadline
Team Merger Deadline- Same as the Final Submission Deadline
Final Submission Deadline- March 31, 2025
All deadlines are at 11:59 PM UTC on the corresponding day unless otherwise noted. The competition organizers reserve the right to update the contest timeline if they deem it necessary.

About the Tabular Playground Series
The goal of the Tabular Playground Series is to provide the Kaggle community with a variety of fairly light-weight challenges that can be used to learn and sharpen skills in different aspects of machine learning and data science. The duration of each competition will generally only last a few weeks, and may have longer or shorter durations depending on the challenge. The challenges will generally use fairly light-weight datasets that are synthetically generated from real-world data, and will provide an opportunity to quickly iterate through various model and feature engineering ideas, create visualizations, etc.
